name: customer-interview-planning
normal_output:
Learning objective: understand how facilitators prepare session materials and whether version confusion causes rework. That relationship is a hypothesis, not an established problem. Recruit people who recently prepared workshop materials, including those who report that the process works well.

25-minute guide:

0–3 minutes: explain the research purpose, voluntary participation and internal note use. Ask permission for notes; recording is a separate choice.

3–10: “Walk me through preparing materials for your most recent session.” Follow with “Where did the files come from?” and “How did you decide what was ready to use?”

10–17: “What, if anything, needed changing or doing again?” Ask for a concrete example, its consequences and the workaround. Let participants identify causes before asking how they distinguished versions.

17–22: “Tell me about a time preparation went smoothly. What helped?” Ask what alternatives they already use.

22–25: summarize your understanding, invite corrections and ask what was missed.

Capture pseudonymous observations separately from interpretations; minimize identifiers and define retention before sessions. Repeated concrete version-related rework would support further investigation. Smooth counterexamples or different causes would weaken or refine the hypothesis. Small interviews cannot estimate market prevalence or prove app demand.
boundary_output:
Replace “How much time would our brilliant app save you?” with “Tell me about the last time you did the task this app is intended to support.” The actual task must be specified before recruitment or interviewing; it has not been supplied here.

Revised guide:

• “What prompted you to start, and what did you do first?”
• “Which tools or people were involved?”
• “Where, if anywhere, did the process become difficult?”
• “What happened as a result, and what did you do next?”
• “Can you recall an occasion when it went smoothly?”
• “What have you already tried changing?”

Ask for recent examples and observable consequences. Do not name the app as the solution or request hypothetical savings. Before starting, explain voluntary participation and note use, and request separate recording consent if relevant.

Founder friends form a convenience sample and may be unusually encouraging. Use their responses as exploratory evidence, preserve disagreement, and recruit independent people who actually perform the task for stronger learning. These interviews cannot establish market demand, purchase intent or time saved.

name: funnel-analysis
normal_output:
The cohort is comparable: all counts are unique eligible accounts from the same mature weekly cohort, and each stage is a subset of the previous one.

| Stage | Accounts | From prior stage | From signup visits |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Visited signup | 200 | — | 100% |
| Created account | 80 | 80/200 = 40% | 40% |
| Completed setup | 20 | 20/80 = 25% | 20/200 = 10% |

Between visit and account creation, 120 accounts did not progress: a 60% stage drop-off. Between account creation and setup completion, 60 did not progress: a 75% stage drop-off. The first transition loses more accounts in absolute terms; the second has the higher proportional loss.

Setup is therefore a useful place to investigate, without assuming it is the most valuable fix. Inspect the setup definition, errors and eligible-account behavior before proposing changes. The figures alone cannot distinguish friction, lack of intent or measurement issues, and cannot establish a cause, financial value or likely uplift.
boundary_output:
A signup-to-paid conversion rate cannot be calculated from these counts.

The 500 figure counts page-view events this month, which may include repeated visits by one account and is not a count of signups. The 80 figure counts paid accounts from all signup months, so it also has a different cohort and timing basis. Dividing them would mix event frequency with accounts and would not answer the requested question.

Hypothesis: clearer signup-button wording increases signup completion among eligible accounts.

Proposed design: compare the current label with one clearer label, keeping the rest of signup unchanged. Randomize eligible accounts 1:1 at first exposure and keep assignment stable across repeat visits. Specify the exact wording before launch. Analyze assigned eligible accounts under a predeclared exposure rule and avoid cross-device reassignment where identity supports it.

Primary outcome: completion within a fixed follow-up window that must be agreed. Baseline completion is 20%. Guardrails: signup errors, unintended duplicate accounts and indicators that the label creates misleading expectations. Check event validity, assignment balance and sample-ratio mismatch.

There are 400 eligible accounts per month, roughly 200 per arm before exclusions. That informs feasibility but does not determine an adequate sample size. Agree the smallest worthwhile absolute improvement, power, error threshold, sidedness and follow-up window before calculating sample size and duration.

Use a fixed analysis point or a specified sequential method, not ad hoc peeking. If the required duration is impractical, label any smaller pilot exploratory. Adopt only under the predeclared evidence and guardrail rules; otherwise retain or revert the control. This design does not launch a test.

Revise the plan before launch. Stopping the first time a dashboard turns positive makes random fluctuations more likely to be mistaken for evidence. Testing ten variants adds multiple opportunities for a false positive; choosing only the most favorable result compounds that problem.

Proposed confirmatory approach: define one primary outcome, a minimum worthwhile effect and a fixed sample size or duration in advance. Specify the family of variant-to-control comparisons and use a suitable multiplicity adjustment, such as a prespecified family-wise-error procedure. Share control traffic only with an analysis that accounts for the resulting comparisons.

If decisions must be made while data accumulate, use a valid sequential design with an explicit stopping boundary and multiplicity handling. A standard fixed-sample significance readout is not interchangeable with that design.

A simpler option is to narrow variants in a clearly exploratory stage, then confirm the chosen variant on fresh randomized traffic. Report all variants, exclusions, guardrails and stopping decisions. normal_output:
Decision: do not adopt the variant under the stated protocol.

Control converted 20 of 100 accounts: 20%. Variant converted 22 of 100: 22%. The observed absolute difference is +2 percentage points; the relative change is +10% compared with the control rate. These descriptive calculations use compatible denominators.

The test was randomized and both groups were fully observed, with equal reported group sizes. The observed difference is below the protocol's requirement for convincing evidence of at least a 3-percentage-point improvement. No confidence interval or other inferential calculation was supplied or performed here, so this readout does not label the result statistically significant or claim an uncertainty bound.

Retain the control under the protocol. This is not proof that the variant has no effect; it means the supplied result does not satisfy the adoption condition. Guardrail outcomes, eligibility checks and any protocol deviations are not supplied and should be included in the final experiment record. Any additional test should have its own prospective sample-size and decision plan, rather than simply extending this completed test until a favorable result appears.
boundary_output:
The comparison shows an observed difference, not a proven causal lift.

Variant: 30/100 = 30%. Control: 20/100 = 20%. The absolute difference is +10 percentage points. Relative to the control, the observed difference is +50%.

However, variant exposure occurred on weekends and control exposure on weekdays. Treatment and day type are confounded: differences in audience, intent or behavior by day could explain some or all of the observed gap. Equal group sizes do not remove this confounding, and a significance calculation would not repair the design.

Supported wording: “The weekend variant group converted at 30%, compared with 20% in the weekday control group. Because exposure timing differed, this comparison cannot isolate the variant's effect.”

Do not publish “proven 50% causal lift” or roll out on that causal interpretation. A stronger next test would randomize comparable eligible accounts concurrently across both weekday and weekend periods, with stable assignment, a fixed outcome window and a predeclared decision rule. No rollout or new experiment has been performed.
